description: We are Twilight Thermal, an already-formed team of Computer Science students working on “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots”. Our skills: Python, FastAPI, machine learning, data science, data handling and analysis, research, frontend development and security analysis. Our team is complete and not accepting new members. We aim to build a validated, clearly explained solution using NASA satellite fire data.
summary:
MODIS has tracked fires from space since the early 2000s. VIIRS is newer and sees fires in more detail (375 m instead 1 km). But the two satellites count fires differently, so their numbers can’t be compared. One fire can look like one dot in MODIS and many dots in VIIRS. The same fire can also be seen many times.
We built Twilight Terminal, a web app that puts MODIS and VIIRS data together into one fire history for Australia, the USA and Canada. We put both satellites on the same 0.25° map grid (about 25 km) and count fires by month. Then we use the years when both satellites worked (2012 onward) to work out how much VIIRS counts differ from MODIS in each country and month. We use that to scale VIIRS to match MODIS. This gives one steady record from 2000 to 2025, no matter which satellite saw the fire. We checked our results against data we did not use for the match (NOAA-20 VIIRS). The typical error was 4.9% for Australia, 6.8% for the USA and 16.1% for Canada. Canada is less accurate because of its winter fires.
In the app, you choose an area and month. You see a fire calendar with colors that are easy to read. You can compare the current period with the average, and download a CSV of the fire data.
This is useful because emergency teams, land managers and scientists need to know when fires happen most and how a fire compares with the past. They can only trust that if the data is consistent.Our app shows this clearly, and explains the method and its limits.
details:
What it does?
Twilight Terminal shows 25 years of fire (2000 to 2025) for Australia, the USA and Canada in one clear record.
MODIS and VIIRS are two NASA satellite instruments that see fire. They do not give the same counts, so you cannot just join them. We put both on the same 0.25° map grid and count fires by month. Then we use the years when both worked (2012 onward) to see how much VIIRS differs from MODIS in each country and month. We use that to scale VIIRS to match MODIS. The result is one steady record, no matter which satellite saw the fire.
In the app, you can pick an area on the map or type your own coordinates, and see a fire calendar as a circle or a grid. You can see which months are above or below normal, see how sure we are about each count, and download a CSV.

Why it helps?
Emergency teams, land managers and scientists can see which months and years burn most, and how a current fire compares with the past. We test our results on NOAA-20 data that we did not use for the match. The typical error is 4.9% for Australia, 6.8% for the USA and 16.1% for Canada. Canada is less accurate because of winter fires, and we say this in the app.

What we used?
NASA FIRMS data. Python, FastAPI and Supabase PostgreSQL for the backend. React, TypeScript, MapLibre and deck.gl for the frontend. Free map tiles from CARTO. An AI assistant (Claude) helped with planning, code and writing. The team reviewed it and made the final decisions.

What is special in it?
The circle calendar shows fire seasons clearly. We show uncertainty, not just one number. We kept NOAA-20 out of the totals so no fire is counted twice. The calendar also marks the 2012 satellite change, so people do not mistake it for a real change in fire.
